prompt.context: A group of 50 investors is considering purchasing a chateau in France and converting it into a bed-and-breakfast (B&B). The purchase price is $1M. The investors plan to renovate and furnish the property. Each of the 50 investors will pay $15K upfront for the right to use the chateau for 2 weeks per year. The remainder of the investment will be financed with bank debt.
prompt.question: Estimate the chateau's financials. Will it make money? Would you invest?

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost of renovations and furnishings?
clarifying_info.a: $250K for renovations and $250K for furnishings, bringing total initial investment to $1.5M.

clarifying_info.q: How is the initial investment financed?
clarifying_info.a: 50 investors x $15K = $750K from investors; the remaining $750K is bank debt.

clarifying_info.q: What is the interest rate on the debt?
How many rooms does the chateau have?

clarifying_info.a: Provide cost components only if specifically asked: proprietor salary $40K, landscaping $10K, laundry $10K, marketing $10K, breakfast $10K, utilities $5K, miscellaneous $15K, plus $75K interest — total $175K/year.

clarifying_info.q: What do competitors charge per night?
clarifying_info.a: Local area B&Bs charge $50-$125/night; castle B&Bs elsewhere in France charge $300-$500/night; upscale Paris hotels charge $400-$500/night.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average occupancy in the region?
clarifying_info.a: Local tourist offices say 50% is average, confirmed by key competitors.

framework: Structure the investment decision as a profitability analysis: Is the chateau profitable? What are the risks?
Identify the three components of initial investment: purchase price, renovations, furnishings
Break down annual operating costs into major buckets: debt service, labor, services, marketing, food, utilities, misc
Estimate revenue as price per night x occupied nights, and determine breakeven occupancy
Compare breakeven to market occupancy benchmarks
Assess risks and qualitative factors before making an investment recommendation

questions.prompt: What are the components of the initial investment and how is it financed?
questions.guidance: Strong answer identifies three cost components (purchase $1M + renovations $250K + furnishings $250K = $1.5M total). Then notes 50 investors x $15K = $750K equity, leaving $750K in bank debt. Better answers note that investor contributions are pre-sold weeks of use, not pure equity.

math.setup: Initial investment = purchase + renovations + furnishings; Financing: investor equity + bank debt
math.answer: Total initial investment: $1.5M; financed 50% by investors ($750K) and 50% by bank debt ($750K)

questions.prompt: What are the annual operating costs?
questions.guidance: Candidate should proactively identify major cost buckets before drilling into assumptions. Strong answer covers debt service, staff, services, food, utilities, and misc. Uses round numbers and reasonable assumptions.

math.setup: Annual costs = debt service + labor + outsourced services + variable costs + marketing
steps: Landscaping: $1K/month x 10 months or ~50 hrs/month x $20/hr x 10 months = $10,000
Breakfast: 5 guests x 400 days = 2,000 breakfasts x $5 = $10,000

questions.prompt: Can the chateau generate enough revenue to cover costs? What is the breakeven occupancy?
questions.guidance: Candidate should determine a price per night using competitor benchmarking, then compute total potential room-nights and required occupancy. A better answer recognizes that investor weeks reduce available commercial nights. A superior answer asks who the right competitor is and reasons about the customer.

math.setup: Revenue = price/night x occupied nights; Breakeven occupancy = total costs / maximum revenue
steps: Price estimate: $200/night (candidate-chosen; reasonable if supported by logic)
Revenue at 50% occupancy (no investor adjustment): $480,000 x 50% = $240,000 > $175,000 costs — PROFITABLE
Adjust for investor weeks: 50 investors x 2 weeks x $1,400/week = $140,000 of in-kind usage
50% of commercial potential: $340,000 x 50% = $170,000 < $175,000 costs — marginal
math.answer: At $200/night and without the investor week adjustment, the chateau is profitable at ~50% occupancy. Accounting for the 50 investors' pre-sold 2 weeks each, commercial revenue at 50% occupancy ($170K) barely covers $175K in costs — the investment is marginal and highly sensitive to occupancy assumptions.

questions.prompt: What are the key risks of this investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify both operational and strategic risks. Strong answers cover at least 2-3 distinct risk categories.

questions.prompt: If the chateau is doing well and returning over $100K profit per year, what should the investors consider doing next?
questions.guidance: Candidate should think about both deepening the current investment and expanding. Good answers consider prioritization criteria for expansion.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the risks associated with investing in this chateau?

categories.name: Occupancy / Revenue Risk
ideas: Remote or non-ideal location makes it hard to attract guests
Overestimated price per night relative to local competition
Investor weeks reduce commercial inventory significantly

categories.name: Execution / Operational Risk
ideas: Delays with French contractors during renovation
Budget overruns on renovation and furnishings
Difficulty finding and retaining a capable proprietor
Managing a property from a distance

categories.name: Exit / Liquidity Risk
ideas: Hard to find a buyer if the investment does not work out
Illiquid asset — real estate in rural France has a limited buyer pool
Investors locked into 2-week annual usage commitments

categories.name: Competitive / Market Risk
ideas: Local area competitors at lower price points ($50-$125/night) could undercut
Higher-end castle B&Bs elsewhere in France set a high bar for quality
Macro tourism downturns could reduce French rural travel demand

recommendation: At $200/night and 50% occupancy (regional average), the chateau barely breaks even once investor weeks are accounted for — the investment is marginally viable at best
The upside case (occupancy above 50%, or higher pricing justified by superior positioning) is possible but requires an active marketing plan and strong execution
Do NOT invest without clearer answers on management quality, a detailed marketing plan, and evidence from comparable B&B investments in France
risks: Occupancy may not reach 50% given the small marketing budget and non-ideal location
Budget overruns or contractor delays could increase the $1.5M initial investment
Illiquid asset with limited exit options if the business underperforms
next_steps: Commission primary research: survey potential customers and interview local B&B operators
Evaluate management options — identify a candidate proprietor before committing
Develop a detailed marketing plan with a defined customer acquisition strategy

If investing, prioritize paying down the $750K bank debt once the business reaches profitability, then evaluate acquiring additional castles (prioritize by size for better unit economics and by geographic proximity to leverage existing contractor relationships)
